transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that regular exercise can significantly improve memory and cognitive function in older adults, according to researchers at the University of British Columbia. The study followed over 100 adults aged 60 to 80 who were experiencing mild memory problems. Half of the participants took part in a twice-weekly aerobic exercise program for six months, while the other half did stretching and toning exercises. The researchers found that the aerobic exercise group showed significant improvements in memory and executive function—skills like planning, organizing, and multitasking—compared to the stretching group. Brain scans also showed changes in the hippocampus, the part of the brain involved in memory, in the exercise group. Researchers say that exercise increases blood flow to the brain and stimulates the release of chemicals that help brain cells grow and connect. They emphasize that it's never too late to start exercising, and that even moderate exercise can have significant benefits for brain health as we age.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of Stockholm in Sweden has announced plans to become the world's first carbon-neutral capital by 2030, five years earlier than its original target. The city has already made significant progress in reducing its carbon emissions, having cut them by over 60 percent since 1990. The new plan includes measures like converting all public transportation to run on renewable energy, making all buildings more energy efficient, expanding cycling infrastructure, and increasing the amount of green space in the city. Stockholm is already known for its commitment to sustainability and its high quality of life. The city says that becoming carbon neutral will not only help fight climate change but also improve public health, create jobs in green industries, and make the city an even better place to live. City officials say they hope Stockholm's example will inspire other cities around the world to take action on climate change. The plan also includes measures to ensure that the transition to carbon neutrality is fair and benefits all residents, including low-income communities.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists at Harvard University have developed a new type of robot that can walk, climb, and even fly, using a combination of legs and small wings. The robot, which is about the size of a housefly, is inspired by insects and can move in ways that traditional robots can't. It can walk across rough terrain, climb walls, and even take off and fly short distances, making it incredibly versatile. Researchers say this type of small, agile robot could be useful in all kinds of situations, like search and rescue operations in disaster zones where it's too dangerous for humans to go, or for inspecting hard-to-reach places like pipes or machinery. The robot is still in the early stages of development, but researchers are working on making it even more capable and adding new features like sensors and cameras. They imagine that in the future, swarms of these tiny robots could be used to explore areas that are too small or too dangerous for larger robots or humans.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Zoe): Hey Jake, I heard you're learning how to cook. How's that going?
Man (Jake): It's going... okay, I guess. I'm still really bad at it, but I'm trying.
Woman: Why did you decide to learn to cook? I remember you used to eat takeout every night.

Man: Yeah, well, my doctor said my cholesterol is too high and I need to eat healthier. Takeout is so greasy and salty, and I'm gaining weight. So I figured if I cook at home, I can control what goes into my food and make it healthier.
Woman: That's a great reason! Cooking at home is definitely healthier than eating out all the time. What have you been making?
Man: Oh, just simple stuff. I tried making pasta last week, and it turned out okay. And I made scrambled eggs for breakfast this morning—they were a little burnt, but edible.
Woman: Ha, that's a start! Everyone burns eggs when they're first learning. Do you have the right equipment?
Man: I don't think so. My knives are really dull, and I only have one frying pan. And my cutting board is tiny. I feel like I'm working in a toy kitchen.
Woman: Yeah, having good equipment makes a big difference. You don't need anything fancy, but a good sharp knife and a decent pan go a long way. Do you have any cookbooks or anything?
Man: No, I've just been watching videos online and following recipes I find on the internet. But it's hard because I don't always know what the terms mean. Like, what's "sauté" anyway?
Woman: Ha, sauté is just cooking something quickly in a little oil or butter over medium-high heat. It's not that complicated. You'll pick up the terms as you go.
Man: I hope so. Another problem is that I'm cooking for just one person, so I end up buying all these ingredients and then they go bad before I can use them. It feels like such a waste.

Woman: Oh, I know what you mean. Cooking for one is tricky. You could try making bigger batches and eating leftovers for a few days. Or you could freeze portions for later. That way you don't waste food and you always have something ready to eat.
Man: That's a good idea. I never thought about freezing things. What else do you think I should know?

Woman: Hmm... don't be afraid to make mistakes. Everyone burns things or messes up recipes when they're learning. The important thing is to keep trying and have fun with it. And start simple—don't try to make some complicated French dish on your first day. Master the basics first.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. Hey, would you maybe want to cook together sometime? You're a really good cook, and I could learn a lot from you.

Woman: Sure! That sounds like fun. How about this weekend? We can make something simple but delicious, like stir-fry or roasted chicken and vegetables. I'll bring some of my extra tools, and we can cook together.
Man: That would be awesome! Thanks so much, Zoe. I really appreciate it.
Woman: No problem! Cooking is more fun with friends anyway. And who knows—maybe you'll be a great cook someday.
Man: I doubt it, but I'll try.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Ethan): Hey Ava, how's your Etsy shop going? I saw you posted some new jewelry the other day—it looks really nice.

Woman (Ava): Thanks! Yeah, I've been making a lot of new pieces lately. But honestly, the shop isn't doing as well as I hoped. I'm not making very many sales, and I'm starting to wonder if it's worth it.
Man: Oh, that's too bad. What do you think the problem is?
Woman: I'm not sure. I think my stuff is good, but no one seems to be finding my shop. It's like my listings are invisible or something. I don't know how to get people to look at my stuff.

Man: Yeah, getting noticed is the hardest part, especially when you're just starting out. There are so many shops on Etsy, it's hard to stand out. Have you tried using social media to promote your work?
Woman: A little bit. I have an Instagram account, but I only have like 50 followers, and most of them are my friends. I don't know how to get more people to see it.

Man: Social media takes time to build up, but it can be really effective if you do it right. You should post more—like every day if you can. And post different kinds of things: photos of your jewelry, behind-the-scenes shots of you making it, videos of the process... people love seeing how things are made.
Woman: Really? I thought people just wanted to see the finished product.
Man: No, the story behind the product is just as important. People want to connect with the maker and know who's making their jewelry and how. It makes the product more meaningful.
Woman: That's a good point. What else?

Man: You should use hashtags—specific ones, not just #jewelry or #handmade, which are too broad. Use more specific hashtags like #handmadeearrings or #etsyjewelry or #artisanjewelry. And engage with other people's posts too—comment on other makers' posts, join jewelry-making communities... that helps get your name out there.
Woman: Hmm, okay. I'll try that. What about pricing? I'm worried my prices are too high, but I also don't want to sell myself short. It takes me hours to make each piece.

Man: Pricing is tricky. A lot of new makers underprice their work because they don't value their time. You have to remember that you're not just selling materials—you're selling your time, your skill, and your creativity. If your prices are too low, people might actually think your work is lower quality.
Woman: Really? I thought lower prices would mean more sales.

Man: Sometimes, but not always. People associate price with quality. If something is too cheap, they wonder what's wrong with it. You want to price your work fairly—cover your materials, pay yourself for your time, and make a profit. That's how you build a sustainable business.
Woman: That makes sense. I think I might be undercharging. What else can I do to get more sales?

Man: You could try doing craft fairs or local markets. Selling in person is great because people can see and touch your jewelry, and they get to meet you. It's also a good way to get feedback and build a local customer base.
Woman: I've thought about that, but I'm kind of nervous about talking to people.
Man: Oh, it's scary at first, but you get used to it. And it's really rewarding when someone buys something you made and tells you how much they love it. You should try it!
Woman: Maybe I will. Thanks for all the advice, Ethan. You've given me a lot to think about.
Man: No problem! Your jewelry is really nice, you just need to get it in front of the right people. Keep at it, and I'm sure you'll be successful.
Woman: I hope you're right.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of video games is a relatively short but incredibly fast-paced story that has transformed entertainment, technology, and culture in just a few decades. From simple arcade games to complex virtual reality experiences, video games have come a long way since their beginnings in the 1970s.

The first video games were developed in the 1950s and 1960s by computer scientists and engineers, but they were mostly experimental and not available to the general public. The first commercially successful video game was Pong, released by Atari in 1972. Pong was a simple table tennis game with two paddles and a ball, but it was a huge hit and launched the video game industry.

The 1970s and early 1980s saw the rise of arcade games, with classics like Space Invaders, Pac-Man, and Donkey Kong drawing crowds to arcades around the world. This was also the era of the first home video game consoles, like the Atari 2600, which brought video games into people's living rooms.

However, the video game industry crashed in 1983 due to too many low-quality games and market saturation. Many companies went out of business, and people thought video games might just be a passing fad.

But the industry came back stronger than ever in the mid-1980s, led by Nintendo and its Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). Games like Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda became cultural phenomena, and Nintendo revived the home video game market.

The 1990s saw the transition from 2D to 3D graphics, with consoles like the Sony PlayStation and Nintendo 64 bringing 3D gaming to the mainstream. This was also the era when PC gaming became more popular, with genres like first-person shooters and real-time strategy games emerging.

The 2000s and 2010s brought even more changes. Online gaming became mainstream, allowing people to play with friends and strangers all over the world. Mobile gaming exploded with the rise of smartphones, making games accessible to billions of people who had never played video games before. And virtual reality and augmented reality began to move from science fiction to reality.

Today, video games are one of the biggest forms of entertainment in the world, bigger than movies and music combined. They're played by people of all ages, genders, and backgrounds. And they're not just for entertainment—video games are also used for education, training, therapy, and even scientific research.

The video game industry continues to evolve rapidly, with new technologies and platforms emerging all the time. It's hard to imagine what video games will look like in another 50 years, but one thing is certain—they will continue to shape our culture and our lives in ways we can't yet imagine.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Sleep is one of the most important things we do for our health, yet many people don't get enough of it. While we sleep, our bodies and brains are busy repairing themselves, processing information, and preparing for the next day. Getting enough quality sleep is essential for physical health, mental health, and cognitive function.

One of the most important functions of sleep is memory consolidation. While we sleep, especially during deep sleep and REM sleep, our brains process and store the information we learned during the day. This is why getting a good night's sleep before an exam is so important—sleep helps you remember what you studied. Studies have shown that people who sleep after learning something new remember it better than people who stay awake.

Sleep is also crucial for physical health. During sleep, our bodies repair damaged cells, boost the immune system, and regulate hormones. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to a wide range of health problems, including heart disease, diabetes, obesity, and weakened immune function. People who don't get enough sleep are more likely to get sick, gain weight, and develop serious health conditions.

Sleep also plays a vital role in mental health and emotional regulation. When we're sleep-deprived, we're more irritable, moody, and anxious. We have trouble regulating our emotions and making good decisions. Chronic sleep deprivation is also linked to depression and anxiety disorders. Getting enough sleep helps us stay emotionally balanced and cope with stress better.

How much sleep do we need? It depends on age. Babies need the most sleep—12 to 16 hours a day. School-age children need 9 to 12 hours, teenagers need 8 to 10 hours, and adults need 7 to 9 hours. Older adults may need slightly less, but still at least 7 hours.

Unfortunately, many people don't get enough sleep. In our busy, 24/7 society, sleep is often seen as something we can sacrifice to get more done. But this is a mistake—skipping sleep actually makes us less productive, not more. When we're tired, we work slower, make more mistakes, and have trouble concentrating.

There are many things we can do to improve our sleep quality. Having a consistent sleep schedule—going to bed and waking up at the same time every day—helps regulate our body's internal clock. Creating a relaxing bedtime routine, avoiding screens before bed, keeping the bedroom dark and cool, and avoiding caffeine and alcohol close to bedtime can all help improve sleep.
Sleep is not a luxury—it's a necessity. Prioritizing sleep is one of the best things we can do for our health, our productivity, and our overall well-being.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: The history of ancient Olympic Games is a fascinating story that spans over a thousand years and gives us insight into the culture and values of ancient Greece. The ancient Olympics were much more than just a sporting event—they were a religious festival, a cultural celebration, and a symbol of Greek unity.

The ancient Olympic Games began in 776 BC in Olympia, a small town in southern Greece. They were held in honor of Zeus, the king of the Greek gods, and they were part of a major religious festival. According to legend, the games were founded by Heracles (Hercules), the Greek hero, but the historical record shows they developed gradually over time.

The games were held every four years, and this four-year period was called an "Olympiad." The Olympics were so important to the Greeks that they used the Olympiad as a way to measure time. During the games, a truce was called between all Greek city-states, so athletes and spectators could travel safely to Olympia, even if their cities were at war. This "Olympic Truce" was one of the most important aspects of the games, showing how much the Greeks valued the event.

Only free Greek men were allowed to compete in the ancient Olympics—women, slaves, and foreigners were not allowed to participate. Married women weren't even allowed to watch the games, though unmarried women could attend. The athletes competed naked, which may seem strange to us today, but it was part of the Greek ideal of physical perfection and the celebration of the human body.

The events in the ancient Olympics were different from the modern games. The most important event was the stadion, a short sprint of about 200 meters. Over time, more events were added, including longer races, wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and the pentathlon, which included five events: running, jumping, wrestling, discus, and javelin.

The winners of the ancient Olympics didn't get gold, silver, and bronze medals like today. Instead, they were crowned with a wreath made from olive leaves, which was a great honor. Winning athletes were celebrated as heroes in their home cities, and they often received special privileges and rewards.

The ancient Olympic Games continued for over 1,000 years, until they were banned in 393 AD by the Roman Emperor Theodosius I, who was a Christian and wanted to put an end to pagan religious festivals.

The modern Olympic Games were revived in 1896, inspired by the ancient games. While the modern Olympics are very different in many ways—they're international, women can compete, and there are hundreds of events—they still carry on the spirit of the ancient games: the celebration of athletic excellence, the coming together of different peoples, and the ideal of fair competition.
